children.text: Explanatory Remarks

A number of five figures at the left side indicates the location of the key word
in the basic texts. In the case of the SV, the HB and the VN, the first three figures
indicate the page number, and the last two indicate the line number (for example,
SV16026=SV 160,26; HB02314=HB 23,14; VN06110=VN 61,10). In the case of the
PV and the NB, the second figure indicates the chapter number and the last three
figures indicate the karika or sutra number (for example, PV02232=PV, the
Pramanasiddhi-chapter v.232; NB03015=NB, the Pararthanumana-chapter sutra 15.
In the case of the SP, the last two figures indicate the karika number (for example,
SP00015=SP, v.15).

3. In this database, sentences are artificially divided into word-units, although they
involve a phonetic fusion or union in the basic texts. Further, compound words are
divided into their shortest constitutive elements (we use a hyphen to indicate that
hyphenated elements originally form a compound word) with the following
exceptions:

3.1. The prefixes a-, dur-, nih- remain undivided, irrespective of attachment to
words or compound words.

3.2. Suffixes making an adverb, for example -vat, -vasa, are divided. But suffixes
making a possessive adjective, for example -vat, -mat, remain undivided, and terms
such as a numeral+ -dha/-vidha/-prakara remain also undivided.

3.3. Compound words with the suffixes -ta/-tva or -bhava/-bhuta fundamentally
remain undivided. For example: karyakaranabhava/-bhuta/-ta.

3.4. Compound words with evam-, tat-, tatha-, para-, yatha-, su-, sva- in the
wordhead fundamentally remain undivided. For example: evamjatiya, tadutpatti,
tathakrta, paratantra, yathartha, yathasvam, sujnanatva, svabhava.

3.5. Some compound words which are regarded as terminology remain also
undivided. For example: agnihotra, ayogavyavaccheda, arthapatti, padartha,
paramartha, prasajyapratisedha, viruddhavyabhicarin, samanantarapratyaya,
samtanaparinama, samanyalaksana, svabhavapratibandha.

4. Those terms whose wordhead is subject to the Sandhi rules (for example, -d
dhetu-) are cited in their original form (for example, -d *hetu-) for the sake of
using this database to make an KWIC index.

The establishment of a desired object is the means of proof (<s>sādhana</s>); that which brings it about is its component (<s>aṅga</s>); the non-statement of that component, that is, the non-utterance of that component by the debater, is the ground for defeat (<s>nigraha-adhikaraṇa</s>), either because of silence due to lack of response (<s>apratibhā</s>) after having accepted [the obligation to prove], or because of the incapacity of a component of the means of proof.

For indeed, the logical sign (<s>liṅga</s>) is only threefold as a component for establishing what is not directly perceived: essential nature (<s>svabhāva</s>), effect (<s>kārya</s>), and non-apprehension (<s>anupalabdhi</s>). Its substantiation consists in establishing the pervading relation (<s>vyāpti</s>) with the property to be proved and then demonstrating the presence [of the sign] in the property-bearer (<s>dharmin</s>). For example: whatever exists or is produced, all that is impermanent, like a pot and so on; and sound exists or is produced. Here too there is no fixed order, since in both cases the establishment of the desired object is the same. One may also first establish existence in the property-bearer and afterwards establish the pervasion, as: sound exists or is produced, and whatever is such is entirely impermanent, like a pot and so on.

Here the means of establishing pervasion is the demonstration of a proof that invalidates the contrary case (<s>viparyaye bādhaka-pramāṇa</s>). If not everything that exists or is produced were momentarily perishing, then since what is non-momentary cannot perform any causal function (<s>arthakriyā</s>) through either succession or simultaneity, it would have ceased in terms of the defining characteristic of capacity for causal efficacy, and thus would be simply non-existent. For what is devoid of all capacity is said to be without designation (<s>nirupākhya</s>).

Thus, when no invalidating proof (<s>bādhaka-pramāṇa</s>) is shown against the contrary of the provable property of the means of proof, due to the absence of contradiction, even when its occurrence in the contrary case is not observed -- it might be existent or produced and yet eternal -- the doubt is simply not removed. Therefore, due to doubt about the negative concomitance (<s>vyatireka</s>), there would be an inconclusive pseudo-reason (<s>anaikāntika hetvābhāsa</s>).

Nor is exclusion established merely from non-observation, because non-observation of what is remote does not establish absence for one who does not perceive everything, and because even among proximate things some existing objects are not observed.

The invalidating proof, however, operating as follows -- where succession and simultaneity are impossible, there is no capacity whatsoever, and in the non-momentary there is such [impossibility] -- draws [the conclusion of] incapacity, the defining mark of the non-existent. Therefore it is established that whatever exists or is produced is impermanent alone. And by that much, the invariable concomitance (<s>anvaya</s>) of the property to be proved with the mere property of the means of proof is [established], and the defining characteristic of the essential nature reason (<s>svabhāvahetu</s>) is proven.

Here too, if one does not accept non-observation as a valid means of knowledge, then since the pervasion is unestablished solely through the impossibility of succession and simultaneity [demonstrating] incapacity, the prior reason too would suffer from non-pervasion. [Objection:] Here too there is the fallacy of infinite regress at the outset of the means of proof. [Reply:] No, because non-observation, which is the means of establishing absence, is not denied. That non-observation which establishes the contrary of the reason in the contrary of the provable is called an invalidating proof (<s>bādhaka-pramāṇa</s>) because it presents what is contradictory to it. For that reason would be established as non-existent in the absence of the provable only if it were contradicted there by something contradictory to it that possesses valid means of knowledge. Otherwise, if the invalidating [proof] against it is not established there, doubt is irremovable. And not every non-apprehension invalidates an entity. Therein, capacity is established as pervaded by succession or non-succession, due to the absence of any other mode. Therefore, the non-apprehension of the pervader (<s>vyāpaka-anupalabdhi</s>) invalidates capacity in the non-momentary, and since the pervasion is established through the absence of capacity [following from] the impossibility of succession and simultaneity, there is no fallacy of infinite regress.

Thus in the employment of essential nature reasons (<s>svabhāvahetu</s>), the component of the means of proof is substantiated. The failure to substantiate it -- the non-statement of a component of the means of proof -- is the ground for defeat of that debater, because the undertaken object is not established, since even when a reason that is actually capable is employed, its capacity is not demonstrated.

In the case of an effect-reason (<s>kāryahetu</s>) as well, the substantiation of the component of the means of proof [is as follows]: when an effect-sign (<s>kārya-liṅga</s>) is employed for proving a cause, the substantiation is the establishment of the cause-effect relationship between them through the means of knowledge that establish presence and absence. As: this comes into being when that exists; when other causes equally capable of producing it are present but that [particular cause] is absent, this does not come into being. For in this way, its status as an effect of that [cause] is substantiated without doubt.

Otherwise, if one merely shows that in the absence of that, this does not occur, the capacity of this [to be its effect] is doubtful when something else is also absent there. Something else was capable there, and due to its absence, that [effect] did not arise. When that [other cause] ceases, the cessation [of the effect] would be mere coincidence -- like the date-palm fruit born in a country suitable for the mother's marriage, which is absent in other countries where the mother's marriage is absent.

Thus, when substantiated, that [sign] is established as an effect of that [cause]. Having been established, it proves the existence of that [cause] through its own occurrence, because an effect does not deviate from its cause. And regarding non-deviation, the principle is the same for all effects with respect to their causes. Thus the failure to substantiate -- even in the case of an effect-reason, the non-statement of a component of the means of proof -- is the ground for defeat of that debater, because when that [cause-effect relationship] is not substantiated, the status as effect is not established, since something else whose nature does not entail the existence of that [cause] -- in whose presence there is no necessity of the existence of that [cause] -- would [equally apply], and thus the undertaken object is not established, since even when an [actual] effect is employed, this [relationship] is not demonstrated.

In the case of non-apprehension (<s>anupalabdhi</s>) too, the substantiation of the component of the means of proof is the demonstration that the non-apprehension is of something that has fulfilled the conditions for being apprehended (<s>upalabdhi-lakṣaṇa-prāpta</s>), because it is only non-apprehension of that kind that establishes the convention of non-existence (<s>asad-vyavahāra</s>), and because the absence is not established merely when the perception of the cognizer ceases regarding something that has fulfilled the conditions for apprehension.

Therein, the fulfillment of the conditions for apprehension consists in a particular nature and the completeness of the other conditions [of perception]. A particular nature is what is not remote in any of the three kinds of remoteness, what has the form of appearing in the perception of the cognizer through the distinction from what does not have its own form. Such a thing, when not apprehended in the presence of other conditions of perception, is the object of the convention of non-existence. Otherwise, when the sign is present [but the conditions are different], there is doubt.

Here too, the pervasion [is]: everything of this kind is an object of the convention of non-existence. [This is established] because, given the acceptance that some [thing] of this kind is non-existent, there is no distinction in its defining characteristic [from other cases]; for if something of this kind is accepted as non-existent due to [its nature], there is no reason for that [non-existence convention] to apply elsewhere [differently]. For there is no non-apprehension of something of this kind that exists when the other conditions of apprehension are present. But something that, being of this nature, is not apprehended -- 'it does not exist' -- this convention of non-existence has this alone as its ground, because there is no other ground for it.

[Objection:] The distinction from all capacities is the ground. [Reply:] That is so -- it is precisely of that which is distinguished from all capacities that such cognition arises, because there is no means of cognizing it for anything else. And when such cognition occurs, [the statement] 'this is the convention of non-existence' states that as its ground.

[Objection:] The convention of existence arises from cognition, verbal designation, and causal efficacy, and in the contrary case the convention of non-existence. [Reply:] There is indeed the convention of existence from cognition having the aforementioned appearance, and the convention of non-existence in the contrary case.

But regarding what is not an object of direct perception, there might be the convention of existence even from inferential cognition or from some [other source]. The convention of non-existence, however, in the contrary case is inconclusive (<s>anaikāntika</s>), because even when the perception of the cognizer or of another valid means of knowledge ceases regarding a remote object, there is doubt.

And not all cognitions and verbal designations, nor their identity and difference, establish the real existence of a thing or the real existence of the identity and difference of things, since even regarding non-existent things such as past and future objects, or objects that perform manifold or singular causal functions, in order to establish that state [of identity or difference] even in the absence of manifold or singular nature, [cognitions and designations] operate as having manifold or singular forms. [Consider:] '<s>Rājā Mahāsammata</s>, the progenitor of the royal lineage; <s>Śaṅkha</s> the wheel-turning king, the raiser of the sacrificial post created by <s>Mahāsammata</s>; the horn of a hare; form is visible and resistant; and a pot' -- for words like 'visible' and so on, though having multiple objects, are [sometimes] used in a single application.

[Objection:] Even though having multiple objects, the application to one is due to the convergence there of what occasions that [designation] -- namely, [the universal] <s>samavāya</s> (inherence). [Reply:] Alas, how this pitiful category (<s>padārtha</s>) has fallen into toil, serving many relata and gathering many words unto itself from them! Why does it not, through those very differentiations of power by which it serves many relata, also generate many words? For in this way the labor of following an endless chain would be spared. If it is incapable of generating many words, then it should also not serve many relata, for without serving them, even its relation to them is not established.

And as for 'pot' -- let the many [qualities] such as form and the rest, which produce a single causal function, be denoted by a single word. What need is there for postulating a separate entity? For many things can produce a single function, like the eye and so on. We see it as reasonable that a single word may be assigned there for establishing their combined capacity. And the application of words to objects by people is not without purpose.

Among those objects, for those that together or separately have a single purpose -- if a single word is assigned to establish that state, what would follow? Even the singular number is not contradictory for a collective term employed to establish the capacity for [a joint] causal function. Since the capacity of those combined is one, not of each individually, the collective term in the singular denoting one collective is 'pot.' For words denoting universals (<s>jāti</s>), since the power of objects individually and combined is manifold and singular, when one wishes to express manifold or singular power, the plural or singular number may be used at will -- 'trees' or 'tree' -- if there were such a rule that the plural must be used only for many and the singular only for one. For us, however, since words operate regarding conventionally designated objects by the force of convention, there is simply no such attachment [to number].

[Objection:] The manifold-and-singular [entity] form and the rest is capable of generating a single word. [Reply:] Do objects raise words by themselves independently of human activity, or are words assigned to objects by persons for the purpose of communication? If [objects] raise [words] by themselves, then one would consider whether there is a capacity or incapacity of the entity, and that is not tenable. If they are assigned by persons, they would assign as they wish -- what objection is there? And the reason for the assignment has already been stated. Moreover, if form and the rest have no relation with a single word, how can they have a relation with a single substance (<s>dravya</s>) considered to be their substratum? This is merely an attachment to what does not exist.

We do not reject a single word because of the contradiction of a single relation; rather, because form and the rest, which are not different [across instances], would contradict [both] the diverse causal functions and words in pots, blankets, and so on -- those, being of uniform nature, would simply not produce a causal function that is impossible in another collection. Therefore, to express that [function], they could not be denoted even by a single word each. Let someone wish that form and the rest be of uniform nature in all collections.

Does this disregard the testimony of direct perception, which manifests them with mutually distinct appearances? And this is undesirable, since form and the rest are accepted as having different natures in each collection.

If the pot were something other than form and the rest, what would follow? Let it be so -- what prevents a thing that exists, that is directly perceived, that has a nature unlike form and so on, from presenting its own form to cognition through its distinction [from them]? And things that appear with distinction are perceived directly even when not in different locations -- like smell, taste, and so on -- and even when grasped by a single sense -- like wind and sunshine as touch. And this alone is the direct perceptibility of what is directly perceived: the presentation of its own form to cognition through distinction from what is not its own form.

But this pot is a buyer who gives nothing in return -- it does not display its own form and yet wishes to claim the status of being directly perceived. By this, cognitions, words, and so on are also explained, if one wishes to establish [real existence] through them. And there is no failure to perceive the form of what is directly perceived when it is not overpowered, such that a logical sign would be stated for its establishment. And for what is not directly perceived, it is not proper to accept the existence of something for which there is no valid means of knowledge. Therefore, the pot is not something other than form and the rest. Thus, first of all, the convention of existence is not [established] through cognition and verbal designation, nor the convention of identity or difference of existence; and for this very reason, there is no [convention of] the contrary from their contrary.

From causal efficacy (<s>arthakriyā</s>), however, the convention of existence would [follow], but not the convention of identity or difference of existence, since even one thing is seen to perform multiple causal functions -- as a lamp produces cognition, wick-transformation, and the generation of another flame -- and since many things like the eye and so on are seen to perform the single function of [producing] one cognition.

We do not say that the convention of difference of existence follows merely from difference in causal function, but rather from a previously unseen difference in causal function. A causal function that was not seen in something and is then seen elsewhere establishes a difference in existence -- as the causal function of holding water, etc., not seen in clay, is seen in the pot; and the causal function of covering, etc., not seen in threads, is seen in cloth. Thus there is a difference in existence.

Something different is thereby established, but even so, a whole (<s>avayavin</s>) is not established. The difference in causal function arises from the production of a difference in essential nature in the continuum of dispositions (<s>saṃskāra-santati</s>) according to [different] conditions, just as fire has different capacities for burning coarse [fuel], cow-dung, grass, and wood due to the different stages of churning the fire-sticks. Similarly, the difference in causal function in threads and so on arises from the production of a different essential nature according to conditions.

By this, the identity and difference of cognitions and verbal designations are explained. Where it was said that the convention of existence is established through causal efficacy and the contrary through the contrary, that is true. But that very contrary is not established regarding things that have fulfilled the conditions for apprehension (<s>upalabdhi-lakṣaṇa-prāpta</s>). There, even unwillingly, this has come about: that whose capacity, having fulfilled the conditions for apprehension, is not apprehended -- that is the object of the convention of non-existence, since existence has the defining mark of capacity. And even so, what is the superiority of this [formulation] over the earlier one? For capacity is not something different from essential nature; and the non-apprehension of that which has fulfilled the conditions for apprehension is the non-apprehension of the essential nature itself. Therefore, this is just the earlier non-apprehension.

Therefore, whoever accepts the convention of non-existence for something on the basis of this non-apprehension must accept it everywhere where there is no difference, or not at all, because there is no distinguishing feature. And that which is similar elsewhere in the same way is undifferentiated, so let it be the same there too. Thus the pervasion: everything of this kind that is not apprehended is an object of the convention of non-existence.

[Objection:] No one who is not apprehended in any way whatsoever is an object of the convention of non-existence. [Reply:] Then, since nothing ever ceases to have all forms, everything would be useful everywhere at all times. And this could not be: 'this [arises] from this, not from this,' 'this is here, this is not here,' 'this [exists] now, this does not [exist] now,' 'this is thus, this is not thus' -- because there would be no cause for the distinction of any form whatsoever in any way, at any place, or at any time. The world would be without invariable concomitance and exclusion (<s>anvaya-vyatireka</s>), because there would be no difference.

[Objection:] The regularity arises from the differences in the cessation and arising of states. [Reply:] But those very [cessations and arisings] are not possible because there is no convention of non-existence regarding anything, from which such regularity would arise. When the convention of non-existence is accepted regarding some object, one must state whence it [comes]. For there is no other cause of determination than non-apprehension, since non-apprehension alone is the means of determination through both affirmation and negation. If the convention of non-existence is accepted from non-apprehension alone, then wherever it exists, everything should be an object of the convention of non-existence, because there is no distinguishing feature.

[Objection:] Non-apprehension is the cessation of all means of valid knowledge; wherever that occurs, [the object] is accepted as non-existent. [Reply:] The gentle-minded friend of the gods does not endure the toil of investigating means of valid knowledge, which is why he has paid no attention here. For the cessation of inference and so on does not lead to absence, due to deviation; nor does the cessation of all direct perception [lead to absence], because that is unestablished; nor does the cessation of the non-specific perception of one's own [perception apply] to remote objects. Therefore, the particular nature from which one invariably arrives at the convention of existence through a means of valid knowledge -- the cessation of that [particular nature] establishes its convention of non-existence, because the existence of that nature is pervaded by the existence of that means of valid knowledge. And there is no apprehension of an object that has fulfilled the conditions for apprehension other than through direct perception, by which there would be apprehension of it through inference. And without an alteration of its form, there is no alteration of its non-perceptibility; and with alteration, that [thing] itself would not exist.

Moreover, where has this incantation-and-medicine-free magic trick been learned from existence? -- that this [thing], with no arising or destruction of a superior quality, situated without obstruction and not far away, in the very same state of those very sense faculties and so on, of the very same person, is sometimes directly perceived and sometimes not directly perceived, so that sometimes its apprehension is inference, sometimes direct perception, sometimes scripture, given that in this very same state without any superiority these modes are contradictory.

[Objection:] Even without any [overall] superiority, one accepts the difference in behavior due to the cessation of one superiority and the arising of another. [Reply:] That superiority, being intrinsic to it, when ceasing and arising without continuity -- how does it not entail a difference in essential nature, like pleasure and pain? And if there is continuity, what arises or ceases for whom? So this amounts to nothing.

Or rather, if one oneself concedes the arising and cessation of some essential nature, why does one not agree when another says the same thing? [Objection:] Because he accepts generation and destruction without continuity. [Reply:] What is this 'continuity' of an entity in its birth and destruction? [It is] a capacity (<s>śakti</s>). That exists even before birth and after cessation. Therefore this [entity] is not newly born in every respect, nor does it perish as the former [entity]. If that [capacity] is always without superiority, then why has this differentiation of behavior been made as though [the capacity] possessed superiority?

[Objection:] Those states possess superiority. [Reply:] Those states and that capacity -- are they one entity or many? If one, then how would these mutually contradictory [qualities] be conjoined simultaneously in one undivided entity: birth and non-birth, cessation and non-cessation, unity and plurality, perceptibility and imperceptibility, usefulness for causal function and non-usefulness, and so on?

[Objection:] There is a succession -- 'state' and 'capacity' -- hence no contradiction. [Reply:] The friend of the gods, prone to forgetfulness, does not observe the topic at hand. This contradiction was stated on the thesis that capacity and state are one entity, without division. But if there is a division between them, there is no contradiction at all; only it would not follow that the birth and destruction of an entity are with continuity, since for that which has continuity there is no birth and destruction, and for that which has birth and destruction there is no continuity.

[Objection:] Due to the non-difference of the two, there is no fault. [Reply:] What an answer! The venerable one, being led into a strait of faults by attachment to his view, does not even notice himself. For non-difference means identity -- 'those two are [one]' -- and this is a conventional usage based on difference. How then would one conjoin [with it] the characteristics of plurality: non-cessation and cessation, non-manifestation and manifestation, stability and instability, and so on? For this is the difference of entities, and its absence is non-difference, as with pleasure and the rest, and with capacity and state in one entity. Otherwise, in the absence of defining characteristics of difference and non-difference, there would be no determination of difference and non-difference anywhere.

[Objection:] Manifestation within that nature is non-difference; in the contrary case, difference -- as the pot manifesting within the nature of clay is non-different from it, and difference in the contrary case as with pleasure and pain. This is the defining mark of difference and non-difference; hence there is no contradiction. [Reply:] The pot does not manifest within the nature of clay; rather, a certain [entity] that is of the nature of clay is the pot. For there is not only one thing of the nature of clay in the three worlds, due to the difference in the appearance in each cognition and the difference in the nature of substances. For in this way, even the comprehension of difference between it and pleasure and the rest, and between consciousnesses, would be possible if difference were of this kind.

[Objection:] Even granting this, due to the continuity of some self, there is unity. [Reply:] This consequence applies equally to pleasure and the rest, and to consciousnesses. And even in pots and so on, there is no continuity in every respect, because of the absurd consequence of dissimilarity, simultaneous arising, and so on. And no one perceives the pot and [something] of the nature of clay with distinction, such that one could say 'this has manifested here.' For without perceiving the distinction between the base and what is based upon it, such [a statement] is not possible. And since the capacity does not manifest within the nature of the capacity itself, its non-difference from its own self would not follow.

By this, transformation (<s>pariṇāma</s>) is refuted. For even one who would postulate that what is a transformation of something is non-different from it -- the capacity does not transform into itself. Moreover, what is meant by 'transformation'? It is the cessation of one property and the manifestation of another property of an enduring substance. That other property which ceases and manifests -- is it that very enduring substance, or something different from it? There is no other alternative.

If it is that very [substance], then its endurance is not cessation and manifestation, and one must say of whom those [cessation and manifestation] belong. And it is not established that the enduring [substance] has a different property, for that very thing does not become a different property of itself without depending on some distinction.

But if the property is something different from the substance, then its cessation and manifestation do not constitute the transformation of the substance. For the transformation of one thing does not consist in the cessation and manifestation belonging to something different, since that would absurdly apply even to consciousness.

And the designation 'property of the substance' is not established, due to the absence of a relation. For there is no real relation of things other than the cause-effect relation. And there is no cause-effect relation between these two, since what is not of that nature by itself does not have that [other thing] as its cause, and the property is something different from the substance.

[Objection:] Even though they are different things, if the substance is the cause of the property, then since it produces a different property that is an effect, the substance has transformed. [Reply:] That is not contradicted even by the other [view]. For in the cause-effect continuum called 'clay-substance,' when from the prior substance 'lump of clay,' which is the cause, the subsequent substance 'pot' arises as an effect, the convention 'the clay-substance has transformed' is accepted. And there is no alternative for the property other than identity with or difference from the substance; and in both cases there is no transformation.

[Objection:] The property is not the substance itself without distinction, nor something different from the substance; rather, it is a configuration (<s>saṃniveśa</s>), a different state of the substance, like a fist of fingers. For the fist is not the fingers themselves without distinction, since spread-out [fingers] are not a fist; nor is it something different, since it is not apprehended with a separate nature. [Reply:] No, because the fist is a particular [configuration of] fingers. For certain fingers are a fist, not all. For spread-out fingers are not, in their undistinguished nature, the same as fist-fingers, since in both states there would be the absurd consequence of both cognitions. For that very distinction which is intrinsic is the defining mark of a difference of entities, like pleasure and pain. And if the distinction arises from something external, the fingers would be perceived as spread-out only, for there is no altered perception when a thing has not deviated from its own nature upon the arising of something else -- due to over-extension.

[Objection:] But it was said that the state is neither the substance itself without distinction nor something different from the substance. [Reply:] This was said but is not tenable. For there is no mode of a real thing other than identity and difference, since the defining characteristics of those two stand in mutual exclusion in a thing, and the abandonment of one necessarily entails the adoption of the other. And as for fingers -- since they perish moment by moment, the spread-out ones are simply different, and the fist is different. There the words 'fist' and so on have a specific referent, while the word 'finger' has a general referent, like the words 'seed,' 'sprout,' and so on, and like the word 'rice' and so on. Therefore the fingers are spread-out, not a fist.

Now, if the effect were simply non-existent in the cause before [its production], why does not everything arise from everything? For in non-existence there is no distinguishing feature. [Objection:] But if everything exists everywhere, this same fault applies equally. For in existence there is no distinguishing feature either. Or if there is a distinguishing feature, that distinguishing feature would be different from the three qualities (<s>triguṇa</s>), since the distinguishing feature has no invariable concomitance when those [guṇas] are present. And for what already exists in its complete state, what is produced? And there is the futility of the means of production, since there is nothing that needs to be accomplished. [Reply:] If some superiority that is somehow non-existent there arises, how can that superiority, being non-existent there, come into being? Or if it does come into being, everything would arise from everything -- so the objection is the same.

[Objection:] It is not the case that the superiority is entirely non-existent there; it comes into being because it exists in some way. [Reply:] The manner in which it does not exist -- how can it come into being when it is non-existent in that manner? And it has been said that there is no purpose of production for what exists in every way.

Even when the effect, being non-existent, arises from the cause -- whatever has the nature of generating whatever, from that alone is its generation, not from another -- this is the regularity. And that regularity of its nature is from its own cause, so there is a regularity of essential nature that is beginningless.

Moreover, if the pot exists in the lump of clay, why is there no perception of it in that state as there is later, or [why is there no] causal function of it [in that state]? [Objection:] Because the particular manifestation (<s>vyakti</s>) has not yet appeared. [Reply:] Since the very thing that has that causal function and so on has the nature of a pot, and since its form was previously non-existent, how does the pot exist [in the clay]? For the existence of one form does not [constitute] the existence of another form. And non-difference of entities when there is a difference in the appearance of form is not tenable, due to over-extension.

Therefore, that whose essential nature has fulfilled the conditions for apprehension and which is not apprehended, simply does not exist. For there is no non-apprehension of it while its essential nature persists. And its non-persistence is its non-reality. The pervasion of the specific non-apprehension by the ascertainment of the convention of non-existence is [established] as with the mutual non-persistence of the essential natures of pain and pleasure.

Therefore, one who establishes the exclusion of something through non-apprehension must demonstrate that it has fulfilled the conditions for apprehension as described. Having demonstrated [the conditions], stating the non-apprehension is the substantiation in the case of non-apprehension of essential nature (<s>svabhāva-anupalabdhi</s>). In the case of non-apprehension of the pervader (<s>vyāpaka-anupalabdhi</s>) as well, establishing the pervader-pervaded relationship between two properties and then establishing the cessation of the pervader is the substantiation. In the case of non-apprehension of the cause (<s>kāraṇa-anupalabdhi</s>) as well, establishing the cause-effect relationship and then establishing the cessation of the cause is the substantiation. In the cases of apprehension of what is contradictory (<s>viruddha-upalabdhi</s>) as well, demonstrating one of two contradictories and presenting the contradictory is the substantiation.

Thus, in the case of non-apprehension, the failure to substantiate a component of the means of proof -- the non-statement of a component of the means of proof -- is the ground for defeat of that debater, because the provable is not established when it is not substantiated.

Alternatively, that by which an object not accepted by the opponents is proved is the means of proof (<s>sādhana</s>), namely, the aggregate of the statement of the triple-characterized reason (<s>trirūpa-hetu</s>). Its component is the statement of the thesis-property (<s>pakṣa-dharma</s>) and so on. The non-statement of even one of these is the non-statement of a component of the means of proof. That too is the ground for defeat of the debater, since in the non-statement of even one aspect of the reason, there is no establishment.

Alternatively, that which is not a component of that very means of proof -- <s>pratijñā</s> (thesis-statement), <s>upanaya</s> (application), <s>nigamana</s> (conclusion), and so on -- the inclusion of such non-components of the means of proof in the proof-statement is the ground for defeat of the debater, because of stating what is purposeless.

Or, since in the employment of a proof through positive and negative concomitance (<s>anvaya-vyatireka</s>), in both the homologous (<s>sādharmyavat</s>) and heterologous (<s>vaidharmyavat</s>) forms, establishment occurs through the statement of just one, the second lacks efficacy; thus the statement of that non-component of the means of proof is also a ground for defeat, precisely because of stating what is purposeless.

[Objection:] But the thesis-statement, although not a component of the means of proof, must be adopted for indicating the subject matter. [Reply:] No, because it is useless. Even without the thesis-statement, the establishment of the desired object follows from the proof-statement as described; therefore its adoption is pointless. [Objection:] But if without indicating the subject matter there is no arising of understanding, how is the thesis not a component of the proof? For there is no purpose of the statement of the thesis-property and so on as a cause of understanding other than being a cause of understanding. And that is equally present in the thesis-statement, so why is it not [part of] the proof?

[Objection:] Because of the incapacity of [each part] alone, it is not a means of proof. [Reply:] The same applies to the statement of the thesis-property as well; so that too would not be a component of the proof. For from the statement of the thesis-property alone there is no arising of understanding. By this, the arising of doubt is also addressed, since from the statement of the thesis-property alone, when the connection has not been shown, doubt arises. Therefore, the adoption of the thesis-statement in the proof-statement is purposeless, and is a ground for defeat of the debater.

Alternatively, that which is not a component of the establishment of the proof -- an unestablished (<s>asiddha</s>), contradictory (<s>viruddha</s>), or inconclusive (<s>anaikāntika</s>) pseudo-reason (<s>hetvābhāsa</s>) -- the statement of that too is a ground for defeat of the debater, because of adopting what is incapable.

Likewise, the statement of a pseudo-example (<s>dṛṣṭāntābhāsa</s>) that is not a component of the means of proof -- one that is deficient in the provable and so on, that fails to show invariable concomitance, and so on -- is also a ground for defeat of the debater, precisely because of adopting what is incapable. For the connection of the reason cannot be shown through those, and from the failure to show [the connection], there is incapacity.

Alternatively, that property of the object which is the basis of dispute and the occasion for the debate -- that is the component of the means of proof for whose establishment [the proof] serves. The introduction and proclamation of another, uninquired-about particular, apart from that, through pretexts such as dependence on a treatise and so on, for the purpose of confusing the opponent, disrupting [his] capacity for response, and so on -- that too is the non-statement of a component of the means of proof and is the ground for defeat of the debater, because of stating what is not relevant, since the opponent has not inquired about the object together with such a particular. When there is inquiry, there is no fault.

However, one should inquire whether the other object [is relevant] through the chain of subsidiary topics -- those who fall into such [digressions] and so on, who are outside [the scope] -- the opponent and the adjudicators who see according to proper reasoning should simply terminate the debate. For there is no object that is not employed when digressions are being made; for one who argues for the doctrine of non-self (<s>nairātmya</s>), even dancing and singing and so on would be relevant in proving that [doctrine], since there is a [possible] connection.

For example, someone might, preceded by a thesis-statement, do the following: 'There is no self -- we Buddhists say so.' 'Who are Buddhists?' 'Those who have accepted the teaching of the Blessed <s>Buddha</s>.' 'Who is the Blessed <s>Buddha</s>?' 'He in whose teaching the venerable <s>Aśvaghoṣa</s> went forth.' 'Who then is the venerable <s>Aśvaghoṣa</s>?' 'He who [composed] the play called <s>Rāṣṭrapāla</s>.' 'What is the play called <s>Rāṣṭrapāla</s> like?' -- and having made this digression, one would read the <s>Nāndī</s> [prologue], 'Then enters the stage-director,' and would read, dance, and sing. The opponent, being unable to follow all this digression, would be defeated.

The assembly [would say:] this is the manner of investigating reality approved by the good and learned. And thus there can be no conclusion of the matter at hand, since the debate itself would not be undertaken because its fruit would be indeterminate.

And how could there be victory and defeat in such [a procedure], since even the opponent's non-response to such a digression could occur through the pretense of responding at length, and since it would be indeterminate? Therefore, the thesis-statement itself is first of all not proper. How then could there be the introduction of irrelevant particulars and the worthless chatter of explaining those digressions? And all such procedure has been promoted by the dull-witted, dishonest people who are incapable of establishing an object through the force of reasoning. As for example, having proposed that bodies, instruments, and worlds are preceded by a superior person, one proclaims the entire content of the <s>Vaiśeṣika</s> treatise under the pretext of explaining bodies, instruments, and worlds. Or in a debate about whether sound is eternal or non-eternal, the author of a treatise for displaying the elaboration of twelve categories, having composed a thesis conjoining 'a pot' as the second of sound and pot in one of <s>Jaimini</s>'s proposed topics on the eternality of reality, explains the meaning of the twelve categories. All this is a device of the dull-witted for concealing their incapacity; it is not adopted by the truthful, since in the examination of reality, the use of sticks, reliance on results, and so on are improper.

[Objection:] In the proclamation of a play and so on, there is defeat because of going to another topic. [Reply:] Why does this not apply to another uninquired-about [topic] as well? For that too has no necessity for establishing the desired provable property. Just as the establishment of impermanence is impossible without establishing the suffering of conditionedness characterized by dependence on causes and conditions -- but such a property, even though not separately stated, is already subsumed in the property to be proved since it is included in the thesis -- therefore its separate introduction or explanation is not [needed]. Hence, the introduction or explanation at that time of even such an object not inquired about by the opponent, whether in the thesis or elsewhere, is a ground for defeat precisely because of going to another topic. Therefore, only the property actually inquired about should be stated as a component of the means of proof. No digression should be introduced, because of the over-extension [that would follow] from introducing one.

Thus, the non-statement of a component of the means of proof is the ground for defeat of the debater -- when the opponent has demonstrated it to be so. Otherwise, there is neither victory nor defeat for either of the two.

The failure to point out a fault is the ground for defeat of the opponent. When the proponent has employed a means of proof, where the opponent who has accepted the counter-thesis does not point out a fault in that subject matter, he is to be declared defeated.

The faults of a proof are: deficiency (<s>nyūnatva</s>), non-establishment (<s>asiddhi</s>), inconclusiveness (<s>anaikāntikatā</s>), proving the contrary of what the proponent wishes to establish, and the eighteen faults of examples. The failure to point out these, the failure to make [them] known, the failure to demonstrate [them], is the ground for defeat of the opponent.

This [failure may be] because the proof is actually faultless, or, even when faulty, because of the opponent's ignorance or incapacity to demonstrate [the fault]. For even when a faulty proof is stated, it is not proper to establish the defeat of the proponent when the opponent has not demonstrated the fault, since victory and defeat are determined with reference to the mutual impairment of [each party's] capacity. However, the victory of one who does not demonstrate [a fault] also does not exist, since from a pseudo-reason no true understanding arises and [hence the reason] does not establish [anything]. For in the investigation of truth there is no practice of trickery.

[Objection:] If so, why is there not defeat, because of the failure of establishing truth? [Reply:] No, because [the proof] has not been refuted. For refutation by another is his defeat, not the mere absence of establishment, since the absence of establishment does not require a counterpart, as it occurs even when there is no counterpart. And since the counterpart's defeat does not arise from his incapacity to refute, there is no defeat [of the proponent]. Therefore, this one, even though stating an incapable proof, is to be declared undefeated when the other has not demonstrated it to be so.

[Objection:] The debate is of those who wish to win, even in the practice of trickery (<s>chala</s>). [Reply:] No, because the treatises of the good are directed at the domain of disagreement among the wicked. For those who act for the benefit of others do not teach false behavior such as initiating false prattle, self-aggrandizement, denigration of others, and other improper conventions. And the earning of gain, honor, and fame through the denigration of others is not the conduct of the good. Nor is it proper for the authors of treatises and the [members of] assemblies approved by the good to torment beings by handing them over to those who behave thus. And treatises on reasoning are not composed by the good for the acquisition of gain and so on. Therefore, there is no such thing as a debate of those wishing to win that is prescribed by yoga [i.e., proper reasoning]. Rather, the good, acting for the benefit of others, instructing the confused, would follow proper reasoning either through the statement of a sound proof or through pointing out genuine faults -- [placing] the evidence directly before the very person for his awakening. That very following of proper reasoning is the debate of the good. If the seeker of truth accepts the stated reasoning, [well and good]; if he does not accept, another will.

[Objection:] Trickery and so on must be employed by the good for the protection of truth against those who wish to win. [Reply:] No, for then one should also say [that one must employ] nail-scratching, slapping, weapon-blows, setting on fire, and so on. Therefore this is not a superior means of protecting truth. The means of the good for protecting truth is the proclamation of [valid] proof and the refutation of pseudo-proofs; in the absence of that, even through the infliction of harm on others by false prattle, truth is not established. And also by other means of expounding reasoning, [truth] is established among the learned. Therefore, the victory of the proponent is the making known of truth for the benefit of others; and that of the opponent is the removal of false understanding through the showing of genuine faults.

Alternatively, that which is not a fault of the proof -- since even in its presence there is no obstruction to the establishment of the object the proponent wishes to prove -- pointing that out is the ground for defeat of the opponent, because of stating a false objection (<s>mithyā-uttara</s>).

For example, pointing out contradiction, saying that a property which the proponent does not wish to prove but which is provable due to scriptural acceptance -- that its contrary constitutes a contradiction. Or pointing out a thesis-fault saying: 'In your thesis "there is no self," there is a contradiction between the two words of the thesis.' Or pointing out non-establishment, saying that the reason 'sound is impermanent because it is produced by effort' is a particular of the thesis-meaning and hence is 'a component of the thesis.' Or pointing out all the counter-arguments (<s>jāti</s>) such as homogeneity, heterogeneity, equality, and so on as faults -- such pointing out of what is not a fault is the pointing out of a non-fault.

When the proponent has made known that [objection] to be a semblance of a fault, the opponent is to be declared defeated, since in the original thesis the proof is faultless. But when the proof is faulty, there is neither victory nor defeat for either, because truth is not made known and because a non-fault was pointed out. And when the thesis-position has been established without a counterpart, [the proponent] becomes the winner.

Therefore, one who wishes to win should both establish one's own position and refute the opponent's position. Even when the proof stated by the proponent is faultless, if the opponent points out a semblance of a fault, victory and defeat consist only in making known [the objection to be] a semblance of a refutation -- not otherwise -- since even when truth is actually stated, truth cannot be made known without refuting the counterpart. And the opponent too is not [defeated] in this case, since there is actually a false understanding.

This proper definition of grounds for defeat has been stated by us. But it is not [our] view that nothing else is proper.

We have not said that where this definition of grounds for defeat as stated does not apply, it is improper for it to be a ground for defeat.

Regarding [the ground for defeat called] 'the concession in one's own example of a property of the counter-example constitutes abandonment of the thesis' -- having refuted the view of the <s>Bhāṣyakāra</s> [commentator] here, the <s>Vārttikakāra</s> [sub-commentator] states this as his settled position. We address precisely that.

When [the debater] concedes in his own example the property of the counter-example, he is to be known as defeated. An 'example' (<s>dṛṣṭānta</s>) is what is seen and established at the end. 'One's own example' is one's own thesis (<s>sva-pakṣa</s>); the 'counter-example' is the opposing thesis (<s>pratipakṣa</s>). One who concedes in one's own thesis the property of the opposing thesis is defeated. For example, one who says 'sound is impermanent because it is perceptible to the senses,' when the opponent objects through [the counter-example of] the universal, says 'if the universal is perceptible to the senses and eternal, let sound also be so' -- this is the abandonment of the thesis, because of abandoning the previously stated impermanence of sound.

Here, what specific restriction is made by this mode [of stating it] -- that the abandonment of the thesis [consists in] abandoning the thesis in this manner? For it is possible to abandon one's own position and adopt the opponent's position in other ways as well, such as through pointing out a fault in the reason and so on, or through stating a counter-proof. And this very thing is the principal ground of the abandonment of the thesis: when demonstrated thus, the thesis must be abandoned, and in abandonment there is defeat.

But this is entirely incoherent -- that when it is said that the universal is eternal and perceptible to the senses, [the debater says] 'let sound also be so.' What sane person, having himself said 'sound is impermanent because it is perceptible to the senses, like a pot,' would accept sound as eternal merely because of the [counter-]example of the universal? Even though the universal is eternal and perceptible to the senses, since there is [also] perception in the impermanent pot, he would [at most] be in doubt.

[Objection:] Out of stupidity he might accept [it]. [Reply:] Even so, what is accomplished by showing the universal? One should simply say 'sound is eternal' to the stupid person, since in the understanding of the stupid there is no analysis.

And when one who accepts in sound the property of the eternal universal that has been shown does not thereby concede the property of the counter-thesis -- and for one who says 'sound is impermanent,' the direct counter-thesis would be 'sound is eternal,' not 'the universal is eternal.'

Therefore, since perceptibility is present in both the eternal and impermanent theses and hence deviates, [the debater] deserves defeat for adopting a non-component of the means of proof [i.e., an inconclusive reason], not because of abandonment of the thesis through concession of the counter-thesis property in this manner.

'Thesis-modification' (<s>pratijñā-antara</s>): when the thesis-meaning is negated through the differentiation of properties, [the debater] states a different thesis. The thesis-meaning as stated is 'sound is impermanent because it is perceptible to the senses.' When its negation is effected by showing the deviation of the reason, [the debater], by differentiating the properties of the universal and the pot through the distinction of being omnipresent and non-omnipresent, makes a different thesis, such as: 'the pot, being non-omnipresent, is impermanent; sound too, being non-omnipresent, is impermanent.' This is called 'thesis-modification,' a ground for defeat because of failure to understand the capacity of the means of proof. For he states the latter thesis 'sound is non-omnipresent' for the purpose of proving the former thesis 'sound is impermanent.' To show this, he says 'statement for that purpose.' The statement for that purpose means the stating of the latter thesis for the purpose of establishing the previously stated provable. And since a thesis is not capable of proving another thesis, it is a ground for defeat.

Here too, one who says thus does not state the thesis-modification for the purpose of proving the former thesis; rather, it is a qualification of the reason. When the deviation of the reason 'perceptibility to the senses' has been pointed out through its occurrence in the universal, by adopting the qualification of non-omnipresence for the reason, he removes the deviation. He does not state a different thesis, since non-omnipresence is already established in sound, and since a thesis has the defining characteristic of indicating what is to be proved.

And what was said -- that he states a later thesis for proving the earlier thesis -- that too is improper. For a thesis stated for the purpose of proving a thesis does not become a different thesis; rather, it is nothing other than a reason and so on. Since it is adopted for the purpose of proving the provable, it would be a statement of the means of proof, not a statement of the provable. And since the property of the reason, namely the example-homogeneity and so on, is present in non-omnipresence, while the property defining a thesis is absent, what is employed in non-omnipresence has the nature of a reason, not of a thesis-modification. And it is utterly incoherent [to say] he states a thesis for the purpose of proving a thesis. For one who, having stated a thesis first, knows how to state a reason, example, and so on, knows something of the sequence of a proof; and knowing [this], how would one of sound mind adopt a thesis for the purpose of proving a thesis? And if he did adopt it, he would desire establishment by thesis alone, and then he should not have stated a reason even before [the modification].

Since it is impossible to enumerate all incoherent [statements] of this kind, even the restriction of the definition is incoherent -- that the statement of a different thesis is a ground for defeat called 'thesis-modification.' Incoherent statement is a ground for defeat -- for all such kinds, a single definition should be stated. And no such behavior has been previously seen in debates, for which effort would be made. And a treatise does not proceed by targeting the prattle of children; and if it did, what would be the end, since [such prattle] is boundless. And it is seen that even the learned sometimes state something unestablished due to insufficient analysis. It is from seeing [actual] behavior that such a ground for defeat is established.

Therefore, here too, if when the proponent has completed [his argument], the other were to point out inconclusiveness, since the inconclusive [reason] is a non-component of the means of proof, it is a ground for defeat of the proponent -- but only if the opponent can establish through a valid means of knowledge that the universal exists, is perceptible to the senses, and is eternal. When one points out [such a fault] based merely on scriptural acceptance without supporting it with a valid means of knowledge, since in the failure to establish these objects by a means of knowledge there is no pointing out of a genuine fault, there is no defeat merely from acceptance, because there is no establishment of the matter by the opponent having demonstrated the fault. But from stating a proof not supported by valid means of knowledge, [the proponent] is not a winner either.

However, when the proponent has not completed [his argument], there is no fault whatsoever in stating a qualification of the reason, since it is an attempt to substantiate the reason.

'Thesis-reason contradiction' (<s>pratijñā-hetu-virodha</s>): this is the contradiction between the thesis and the reason. For example, the thesis 'substance is distinct from qualities' and the reason 'because a thing different from form and the rest is not apprehended' -- this is a contradiction between the thesis and the reason. By this very [category], 'thesis-contradiction' is also stated -- where the thesis contradicts its own words, as [in] 'the female ascetic is pregnant' or 'there is no self.' And 'reason-contradiction' too -- where the reason contradicts the thesis, as [in] 'everything is separate, because of the use of the word "being" in a collection.' By this, the contradiction of the example with the thesis is also explained. And the contradiction of the reason with the example and so on, and the contradiction with a valid means of knowledge, are to be stated for the thesis and reason.

[Objection:] There is contradiction because in the opponent's thesis, pointing out inconclusiveness with one's own established [entity] such as cowness and so on [constitutes] a contradictory counter-argument (<s>viruddha uttara</s>). Whoever charges inconclusiveness against the opponent's thesis with one's own established [entity] such as cowness -- that should be known as a contradictory counter-argument and also as one neglecting one's own thesis. And whoever employs a reason without regard to one's own thesis, [such as] 'sound is impermanent because it is perceptible to the senses,' [is contradicted] because his own established [entity] cowness and so on contradicts impermanence. [When the entity is] accepted by both parties, however, the charge of inconclusiveness is [based on] a matter accepted by both.

Here too, since the employment of the thesis in the proof-statement is prohibited, the contradiction of the reason or example based on or caused by [the thesis] is not [a separate ground], and so 'thesis-contradiction' is not a ground for defeat at all.

[Objection:] It may be argued that even without the employment of the thesis, the contradiction between thesis and reason that is understood [implicitly] still exists. For example, when it is said 'a thing different from form and the rest is not apprehended, and that is distinct from qualities' -- even when stated [without the thesis], the contradiction between the provable and the means of proof is understood: 'How can there be non-apprehension of something different and yet its distinction?'

[Reply:] True, this contradiction would exist if the reason were to prove the contrary of the provable property. For if there is non-apprehension of the own-appearance [of substance], through the distinction from the appearance of form and the rest, of a substance that is accepted as existing and as having fulfilled the conditions for apprehension, then by its absence it does not exist -- since this proves the contrary of the desired exclusion, it is a contradictory reason, which has already been stated by us. So this ground for defeat does exist if such a contradiction between thesis and reason is intended. But if the fulfillment of the conditions for apprehension is denied [for this case], then there is no contradiction between thesis and reason at all, since even for things that are distinct, when they are remote from some [cognizer], their non-apprehension by the exclusion of that [cognizer] does not [preclude] their existence.

What was said -- that there is thesis-contradiction when the thesis contradicts its own words -- in that case, the ground for defeat is precisely this: the employment in the proof-statement of the thesis which is not a component of the means of proof; not the contradiction, since it is based on that. If the contradiction were independent of the thesis, it would be a basis for defeat. But since it is based on the thesis, the defeat is caused precisely by the employment of that [thesis], since the debate concludes with the opening and closing [of the thesis]. Pointing out a contradiction is pointless, because one cannot defeat the already defeated -- like setting fire to what has already been burned to ashes.

But where in discussions of inquiry multiple reasons are stated for one provable, each alternatively functions with the capacity to prove that provable -- otherwise the second would be useless. For if there too the employment of the second were impossible without the employment of the first, then the second would have no proving capacity, because of the absence of establishing what has [already] been established. Therefore, the thesis-contradiction with one's own words is not a ground for defeat at all.

And there is no thesis-contradiction in 'there is no self,' because the meaning of the word 'self' is denied as being an uptake of a real entity. The contradiction would exist if the referent of the word were denied. But the particular (<s>sva-lakṣaṇa</s>) is not the referent of a word.

As for the 'reason-contradiction' that was stated as the invalidation by the thesis -- 'everything is separate, because of the use of the word "being" in a collection' -- there is no employment of the thesis here, nor of the reason, by which there would be a contradiction. Rather, by showing the established meaning, this is a concluding statement: from this [it follows].

Having established through other reasons that words do not denote a single particular and do denote a general [meaning] of multiple objects -- showing that the referent of every word, being of the nature of multiple objects, has no nature as a single particular thing -- one says regarding the referent of words 'everything is separate.' By this, the [alleged] contradiction is answered. And this is an illustration of an example: 'sound is impermanent because of the impermanence of what is produced,' just as. When there is disagreement about some object, having shown the use of a word in the well-known [sense of] a generality of multiple objects, one who has demonstrated the locus of disagreement concludes with the generality 'everything is separate.'

[Objection:] If it is the employment of an example, why was it not employed in the direct order of that employment, and why was the subject of disagreement not shown? [Reply:] No, because of the summary statement, and because even thus the employment is seen, and because it is a proof-statement. For this very reason, there is no invalidation of the reason by the thesis. And no one who says 'there is not even a single thing' wishes for a single collection having the nature of an aggregate, by which there would be a contradiction.

Even one who states the division of the atom through [the argument of] 'contact with six [atoms] simultaneously' and so on does not wish to establish a single [entity] having the nature of an aggregate; rather, [he wishes to establish] precisely the non-existence [of the atom], through the negation of both unity and plurality. Therefore, that [collection] too is not intended by him, [the word] is not applied there, and hence there is no contradiction.

[Objection:] This contradiction does not differ from the earlier 'thesis-reason contradiction,' so why is it stated separately? There, the thesis and reason invalidate each other; here, the thesis [invalidates] the reason -- there is a difference. [Reply:] Contradiction of meaning would [allow] a relation of invalidation between the reason and thesis. And every contradiction of meaning in two [propositions] is mutually invalidating, since the proximity of one meaning precludes the possibility of the other. Therefore, in the separate illustrations of invalidation between reason and thesis, there is no difference in meaning.

Moreover, this [reason], whether contradictory or non-contradictory, when the reason is employed, is non-established due to being in a different locus -- so non-establishment of the reason is the ground for defeat. For when it is stated, being understood as not having that property, it brings about the defeat of the speaker. And when he is defeated thereby, there is no point in considering the contradiction of meaning.

Moreover, this contradiction between thesis and reason, being possible everywhere, does not go beyond the twofold class of reason-faults: contradictoriness (<s>viruddhatā</s>) and non-establishment (<s>asiddhatā</s>). Contradictoriness: when the reason's presence in the property-bearer is established, there is precisely the presence of the contrary of the provable property -- this is thesis-contradiction. Non-establishment, on the other hand: when the property of the property-bearer asserted in the thesis is [to be] established, since contradictory natures cannot coexist in one [locus]. And there is no other [kind of] contradiction.

[Objection:] When the nature of the property-bearer is unestablished, from the contradiction of the stated reason-meaning and thesis-meaning, contradiction is possible. [Reply:] But when there is no connection with a valid means of knowledge for both regarding the property-bearer, there is doubt. In that case, since there is doubt about the presence of the reason in the property-bearer, the reason-fault is precisely non-establishment. Thus no contradiction other than non-establishment and contradictoriness is a cause of defeat. And since the contradictory and the non-established are already stated as pseudo-reasons, 'thesis-contradiction' need not be stated separately.

[Objection:] Since contradiction is based on both, according to one's intention one or the other is stated. [Reply:] This might be so -- the contradiction between thesis and reason, being based on both the thesis and the reason, is based on both. When thesis-contradiction is intended, it is called 'thesis-contradiction'; when the contradiction is of the thesis or the reason, [it is called] 'contradictory reason.' Hence there is no fault in [calling it] either thesis-contradiction or reason-contradiction. The illustration of reason-contradiction: 'sound is eternal because it has the property of being produced.' Of thesis-contradiction: 'there is no self.' Of the mutual contradiction of thesis and reason: 'substance is distinct from qualities,' and so on. Of the illustration of reason-contradiction by the thesis: 'there is no single entity,' and so on.

[Reply:] No, because contradiction, being dependent on the reason in every case, does not transcend the pseudo-reasons, as stated before. And when a mere thesis-contradiction independent [of the reason] is intended, the mention of the reason in 'thesis-reason contradiction' is incoherent. And 'reason-contradiction' is also not proper in 'it is eternal because it has the property of being produced,' for reason-contradiction is when the thesis invalidates the reason. Here, however, the reason invalidates the thesis, so thesis-contradiction is appropriate, since even when the contradiction is based on both, the determination of that contradiction is by what is being invalidated.

As for what was said -- that by this, the contradiction of the example with the thesis and so on should also be stated, after the manner of a figure in a painting (<s>bhaṇḍālekhyanyāya</s>) -- there too, contradiction would exist in an example that has the contrary of the thesis-property. And in a contradictory example: if the occurrence of the thesis-property is established as exclusive [to that example], then the pseudo-reason is contradictory; if the restriction of its occurrence [to the contradictory example] is not established, [the reason is] inconclusive (<s>anaikāntika</s>); and if there is no occurrence [at all], it is uncommon (<s>asādhāraṇa</s>).

[Objection:] When the reason does not occur in the contradictory example and occurs in the contrary, there is no reason-fault but there is example-contradiction with the thesis. [Reply:] No, that too does not exceed being a cause of doubt. For example-contradiction with the thesis is a fault in the homologous example, not in the heterologous, since [the heterologous example having the contrary property] is accepted. And in a homologous example having the contrary property, even though the reason does not actually deviate from the provable, the non-deviation property cannot be shown; therefore, from a reason whose invariable connection has not been shown, there is no certainty. Hence example-contradiction with the thesis does not transcend the pseudo-reasons.

[Objection:] Let there be a fault in both ways. [Reply:] No, because one who has already been defeated by the prior occasion of the reason-fault need not be considered for another fault. Especially for one who maintains a fixed order of proof-components: since the property of the reason, namely homogeneity with the example, is not possible in a contradictory example, [the debater] is defeated by the fault of the previously employed reason, and contradiction by reference to the subsequent example need not be considered. For the reason also, example-contradiction would be either uncommonness or contradictoriness, if there were occurrence in the heterologous [example].

As for the contradiction of the reason with a valid means of knowledge, as in 'fire does not burn because of [its] coldness' and so on -- this is a non-established pseudo-reason.

The contradiction of the thesis with a valid means of knowledge is explained through contradiction with one's own words.

All these proof-contradictions are subsumed under the pseudo-reasons and are thus already stated through the statement of pseudo-reasons.

As for the 'contradictory counter-argument' -- the charge of inconclusiveness against the opponent's thesis with one's own established [entity] such as cowness -- that is simply incoherent. For if one wishes to establish the deviation [of the reason] for the opponent through one's own established cowness and so on, since that is contradictory to one's own thesis, it is not accepted -- so the contradiction would be proper. For he himself, being in doubt about the occurrence of the reason in his own accepted cowness, thus reveals his own non-understanding. And that reason, whether cowness exists or not, without its proving capacity being established, is inconclusive because it causes doubt. But when the capacity is established, if the reason does not occur in cowness, there is no doubt at all, since the substantiation removes all modes of doubt. By this, the inconclusiveness of the employment of a reason without regard to one's own thesis is explained -- he too, asserting a reason that occurs in his own accepted eternal cowness [to prove] impermanence, states what is, due to the non-substantiation of a component of the means of proof, merely a cause of doubt. And what was said -- that the charge of inconclusiveness with a matter accepted by both parties [constitutes a contradictory counter-argument] -- there too the inconclusive must necessarily be stated through the avenue of being a cause of doubt. When that is not substantiated, it is the same elsewhere too; hence there is no difference between the inconclusiveness [based on] what is established by both and [based on] either [party].

As for what was said -- that since pseudo-examples are preceded by pseudo-reasons, they are already stated through the statement of those [pseudo-reasons], and hence need not be stated separately among the grounds for defeat -- that too is improper for one who maintains a separate proof-component called 'example.' For one who holds the example as a separate component of the reason -- his statement of pseudo-reasons does not entail the statement of pseudo-examples, because if what is conveyed by the statement of one were entailed by that [other], then there would be the absurd consequence of the absence of any other component of the proof. Since the pseudo-examples are subsumed under the pseudo-reasons, the example itself should be subsumed in the reason, and then the example would not be a separate component of the proof, since it does not function separately.

What the example is meant to prove -- that is subsumed in the reason, and is thus proved by the reason alone; hence the example has no separate capacity.

Moreover, since there is no proper ground for defeat of a thesis-proponent without involvement with a pseudo-reason, all [grounds for defeat] related to it are already stated through the statement of pseudo-reasons alone, and need not be stated separately. Even going to another topic and the rest are possible [only] when the reason is incapable. For no one undertakes going to another topic when the reason is capable and the provable is established; it is [only] one whose [reason] is incapable who engages in false activity.

'Thesis-abandonment' (<s>pratijñā-saṃnyāsa</s>): the withdrawal of the proposed object upon the negation of the thesis. When one who has proposed 'sound is impermanent because it is perceptible to the senses,' upon the negation being effected by the demonstration of the deviation of the reason through its occurrence in the universal, [says] 'Who says sound is impermanent?' and abandons [the thesis] -- this is the ground for defeat called 'thesis-abandonment.'

Here too, if even when the deviation of the reason is pointed out, he does not abandon his thesis, why is he not [simply] caught? [Objection:] He is already caught through the statement of a pseudo-reason. [Reply:] Then what need is there for the further consideration of thesis-abandonment? That very [fault] is his primary ground for defeat. What is the use of these other indeterminable [categories], these impotent prattle-gestures? For thus, by enumerating [further consequences], there would be an over-extension. When the thesis is negated, [one could say] 'the silence of the one who falls silent is a ground for defeat called silence,' 'the fleeing of the one who flees is a ground for defeat called flight,' and so on -- all this could be stated as well. Therefore this too is incoherent.

When the reason that was stated without specification is refuted, [the debater] wishing a specification [states] a different reason. The illustration: 'This manifest [world] is of one source because of its measuredness; the measuredness of things produced from clay, such as dishes, is observed.' When this is countered by deviation -- 'measuredness is observed in things of many sources and of one source' -- the one thus countered says: 'From the observation of measuredness in modifications that are pervaded by a single source: for all this manifest [world] is apprehended as measured, being pervaded by pleasure, pain, and delusion. In the absence of its being pervaded by the nature of another source, its being of one source [follows].' This constitutes stating a different reason when the unspecified reason is refuted. And when there is a different reason, since the earlier reason is non-establishing, it is a ground for defeat.

Here too, when one is already caught for stating the earlier inconclusive reason, where is the use of considering a different reason? If the one who stated the earlier proof, having stated an inconclusive reason and having been given the opportunity to respond -- he is caught by that very [fault]; if the opportunity to respond has not been given, even in stating a different reason he does not deserve defeat, because [the debate] has not ceased.

'Another topic' (<s>artha-antara</s>): a meaning unconnected with the topic at hand. When the thesis and counter-thesis have been adopted with the characteristics as stated, and the establishment of the provable from the reason is underway, [the debater] might [say]: 'Sound is eternal because of intangibility'; and 'a reason (<s>hetu</s>) is a word formed with the suffix <s>tu</s> from the root <s>hi</s>; and a word is a noun, a verb, a prefix, or a particle' -- and having introduced this, expounds on nouns and so on. This is the ground for defeat called 'another topic,' because it is unconnected with the accepted object.

This is a proper ground for defeat: for both the proponent and the opponent, when a fault has been demonstrated, abandoning the topic at hand [constitutes] non-statement of a component of the means of proof and failure to point out a fault. For when the proponent, instead of substantiating the proof that has been introduced, neglects to do so and introduces some other topic, whether related by digression or not, even the statement of what is not necessarily connected [with the topic] is a ground for defeat.
